text: Mercado Bitcoin, Brazil’s biggest Bitcoin exchange, says it will refund users after a $40 million hack, with customers told they will not bear the losses tied to $BTC holdings on the platform. The refund pledge comes as withdrawals on the exchange remain frozen. No restart date has been announced, leaving users unable to move funds even as the exchange says they will be made whole. That contrast is the core of the story: a public promise that customers won’t pay for the breach, paired with an operational freeze that has no clear end date. Key details remain unconfirmed, including how and when refunds will be processed and what exactly must happen before withdrawals resume. The exchange has not provided a timeline for restoring normal service. text: Liquid Network, a Bitcoin sidechain, says it has restored full $BTC backing two months after a $320 million exploit shook confidence in the project. Blockstream CEO Adam Back said the sidechain’s defenses have been hardened following the incident. He also issued a blunt warning to developers: do not trust AI-suggested fixes blindly. The restoration marks a key step for the network, but details of how the backing was rebuilt remain limited. It is also unclear what specific security changes were made beyond Back’s statement that protections are stronger. text: Bitmine kept adding $ETH as the market absorbed a record Binance theft, with Tom Lee arguing the reaction says more about crypto’s resilience than its fragility. text: BTCPay has told merchants using its Bitcoin payment software to shut down servers after reports of attacks on hot wallets, putting $BTC payment operators on alert. The attacks targeted versions 2.4.1 and older. The merchant warning came days after BTCPay shipped an emergency fix for a critical flaw. Operators are being urged to switch off servers rather than keep exposed systems running while the situation is assessed. The advice matters for merchants that rely on BTCPay to accept Bitcoin payments and may hold funds in connected hot wallets. It is not yet clear how many merchants were affected or whether any funds were lost. The focus on older software versions makes timely upgrades and server isolation the immediate priorities. text: The crypto industry is confronting one of the largest heists ever recorded after attackers tied to North Korea drained roughly $6.4 billion from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange. $LINK That figure alone makes the incident a defining moment for exchange security. It also puts fresh pressure on how large platforms protect customer assets and how quickly suspicious outflows are detected. What is known is the scale and the North Korea link. What remains unconfirmed is the exact attack vector, the timeline of detection, and whether any of the funds have been recovered. Those gaps matter. In major crypto thefts, the first hours often determine whether stolen assets can be traced, frozen, or moved through mixers and bridges. None of those steps has been confirmed here. text: A record $6.4 billion hack has hit Binance, yet $BTC is not behaving like it did after the exchange’s last major breach. Bitcoin fell about 3% after the incident. text: Ethereum’s EIP-7702 is drawing fresh scrutiny because it sits at the center of questions around a $6.4B Binance hack. The proposal matters for $ETH users because it changes what an ordinary wallet can do. EIP-7702 lets regular Ethereum wallets run smart contract code. That is a major shift: a wallet is no longer only a key holder for sending assets, but can also execute programmed actions. The upgrade is described as enabling batched and sponsored transactions. In simple terms, it opens the door to wallet behavior that was previously associated with smart-contract accounts. What remains unconfirmed is the precise role EIP-7702 played in the $6.4B Binance hack. The core proposal itself is about wallet capability, and the link to the hack is the key claim people are watching. For traders and users, the debate is bigger than one feature. text: Trezor is telling buyers who purchased the Safe 5 hardware wallet through CryptoBilis to move their funds after a report claimed the device contained a hardware implant. The wallet maker has not yet inspected the device, but it is treating the report as credible. $MKR The warning puts a spotlight on supply-chain risk in hardware wallets. A device that looks sealed and legitimate can still be compromised before it reaches a user, and buyers often have no easy way to verify the full path from factory to doorstep. Trezor's advice is clear: do not wait for a full teardown or public confirmation before securing assets. Users who bought a Safe 5 via CryptoBilis are being told to transfer funds to a wallet they trust. The report remains unconfirmed, and Trezor has not yet examined the specific hardware. text: Wallets tied to the suspected Binance hack are racing to convert freezable stablecoins into $ETH on decentralized exchanges, on-chain records show. The moves point to a scramble for exit ramps while the trail is still visible. The suspected attacker appears to favor Ethereum over stablecoins that can be frozen by issuers. Swapping into $ETH on DEXs can make funds harder to block quickly, though the activity does not prove the wallets are controlled by the hacker. The timing is sharp: DeFi exchanges have paused markets, adding friction to a route that was already under scrutiny. Pausing markets can slow swaps and give defenders more time to trace flows. What remains unclear is the scale. The exact amount moved and the full list of venues involved are not confirmed. The link to the Binance hack is still suspected, not proven. text: Taiwan’s legislature has approved the Virtual Asset Service Act, its first comprehensive crypto statute, creating a licensing regime for virtual asset firms and a stablecoin framework. The bill now goes to President Lai Ching-te, who is expected to sign it within ten days. For $BTC and the broader digital-asset market, the vote signals another Asian jurisdiction moving from scattered guidance to a single law. Under the act, crypto businesses must win approval from Taiwan’s Financial Supervisory Commission before operating. The framework covers seven provider categories, including exchanges, trading platforms, transfer firms, custodians, underwriters and lending services. Unlicensed operation can bring up to seven years in prison and fines reaching NT$100 million, or about $3.14 million. The stablecoin rules are Taiwan’s first. text: A Bitcoin neobank in the Eurozone has achieved MiCA compliance for a debit card that never takes custody of your $BTC. Wavespace says the card uses a novel protocol to pull sats from your self-hosted Lightning node only when you spend, automating self-custody payments without preloading a custodial account. Traditional crypto debit cards require you to preload a custodial balance, often on-chain, which is slow and manual. If the balance runs out, spending stops. Wavespace's self-custody card instead connects to a user's Lightning node via Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC), a protocol documented in NIP-47. Users set a minimum balance—say $200—and each VISA transaction triggers Wavespace to top up the card from the user's self-custodial wallet. text: Datavault AI, a Bitcoin treasury company, says it has been unable to withdraw its $BTC from Biconomy since June. The disclosure hit the company’s stock as investors digested a custody problem at the heart of its treasury strategy. The company has not said how much Bitcoin is affected or why the withdrawal has been blocked, leaving a key question unanswered: whether the coins are frozen, disputed, or simply inaccessible. No resolution timeline was provided. The custody issue is compounded by an accounting one. Datavault plans to restate four financial reports tied to a $150 million Scilex deal, adding fresh uncertainty for investors who thought they were buying exposure to a Bitcoin balance sheet. text: SK Hynix has posted a record quarter, with quarterly revenue topping 100 trillion won for the first time. The chipmaker is riding a wave of AI memory demand that it says is overwhelming supply. $MKR The company expects memory demand to outrun supply through 2030. That is a striking forecast for an industry that has long swung between shortages and gluts. SK Hynix also says its DRAM and HBM products are sold out through 2029. HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, is a key component in AI hardware, and the sold-out status points to persistent tightness rather than a short-lived spike. The numbers are unconfirmed beyond the company's own outlook, and no independent supply forecast was included in the notes. text: The Federal Reserve kept interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, and $BTC held steady as traders weighed a decision that was not as unanimous as it first appeared. The vote was 10-2. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both favored a rate hike, making the dissents the clearest signal that the central bank is still split on how tight policy needs to be. For crypto markets, the immediate takeaway is that the Fed paused—but the internal disagreement keeps a December rate hike in play. That possibility is not confirmed as a policy decision, and the notes do not provide a timeline beyond the vote itself. Bitcoin’s steadiness suggests traders are not treating the pause as a clean pivot. A split Fed can mean more uncertainty ahead, especially if the next meeting brings another close vote. text: Wall Street’s fast money has been exiting spot Bitcoin ETFs. $BTC exposure at nine hedge funds and banks dropped by 68,000 BTC, a shift tied to the collapse of the cash-and-carry trade. The cash-and-carry trade relied on spot Bitcoin ETF exposure against futures positions. With that spread gone, the incentive for hedge funds and banks to hold the ETF leg disappeared. As those players reduced exposure, wealth platforms and sovereign funds added. That leaves the ETF holder base looking different: fewer short-term arbitrage desks, more longer-horizon allocators. The 68,000 BTC figure is the headline number from Galaxy Research’s tracker. The breakdown between full exits and smaller trims is not clear. What is clear is the rotation: hedge funds and banks cut, wealth platforms and sovereign funds added. That contrast is the story for Bitcoin ETF flows. Tap $BTC to trade. Tap $BTC to trade $BT

text: Keystone is pulling hardware wallet devices after attackers obtained the factory key that proves its wallets are genuine. The incident affected 25,964 buyer records, and it lands squarely on the trust layer for $BTC self-custody: the check that tells a buyer whether a device is real. With that key in the wrong hands, counterfeit devices could be made to look authentic to the same verification process. Keystone says recovery phrases and private keys were not involved, separating the incident from a direct loss of wallet secrets. That distinction matters, but it does not erase the operational risk. A buyer who cannot trust the authenticity check has to treat device sourcing, packaging, and first-use setup as part of the security perimeter, not as an afterthought. Details remain thin. text: The McRib is back at McDonald’s, and some crypto traders are convinced it means a Bitcoin pump is coming. Their bullish case for $BTC appears to rest on fast-food nostalgia and market superstition rather than data. Experts are pouring cold water on the idea. Their assessment is direct: there is no correlation at all between the McRib’s return and Bitcoin’s price. Crypto markets often turn random cultural moments into trading narratives. A limited-time sandwich can become a meme, and a meme can become a trade—even when the fundamental link is imaginary. For now, the McRib-Bitcoin theory is unconfirmed. The round also drew participation from mining-hardware makers Canaan and MicroBT, a signal that equipment suppliers see demand beyond pure Bitcoin hashing. Luxor plans to use the funds to expand into AI compute trading, hardware and derivatives. In plain terms, it wants to build markets and financial tools around scarce compute capacity, not just mine $BTC. Details on valuation, investor terms and timing were not disclosed in the notes. text: Electrum, a widely used Bitcoin wallet, has fixed a critical flaw that could send $BTC straight to attackers. A confirmed exploit allowed malicious servers to replace a pending transaction, making users approve a payment to an address controlled by the attacker. The attack exploited the gap before confirmation, when a wallet shows a transaction as pending. By swapping that pending entry, rogue servers could create the appearance of a normal payment while quietly redirecting funds. The wallet has been patched, but the case highlights a deeper trust issue: users rely on the servers their wallet connects to for accurate transaction data. A single manipulated update can turn a routine transfer into a loss. text: Bitmine, the crypto treasury company associated with Tom Lee, has added 10,452 ETH, lifting its holdings to 4.95% of Ethereum’s supply. The purchase keeps the firm among listed companies using capital markets to build digital-asset exposure. $ETH The bigger signal may be its own equity. Bitmine repurchased 2.04 million of its own shares, a move the company describes as part of the largest equity buyback any crypto treasury company has run. That puts the buyback alongside its $ETH accumulation as a central part of the strategy. Buying more Ethereum while retiring shares shows how crypto treasury firms are juggling two balance-sheet goals: maintaining token exposure and supporting their own stock. text: Spot Bitcoin ETFs pulled in about $301 million in net inflows over the week, ending a two-week losing streak. For $BTC funds, it was a rare positive weekly print after a stretch of sustained withdrawals. But the relief was not clean. Two straight days of outflows late in the week trimmed the weekly total and kept October in negative territory overall. That split matters. It shows investors are willing to step back in, yet conviction remains fragile, with money leaving on consecutive days even as the weekly ledger turned positive. The flow data offers a mixed signal: demand is not absent, but it is not steady either. The week’s net gain broke the streak; it did not erase the month’s red print. text: Bitcoin Core is rewriting its security policy for a world where $BTC bugs can be found with a single AI prompt. The project will now backport fixes and cut releases immediately for flaws flagged as “easily discoverable,” moving away from the long embargoes that once gave developers time to patch quietly. The change targets a new threat model: attackers using AI to surface vulnerabilities quickly, before a slow disclosure process can contain them. Under the revised approach, easily discoverable bugs get fast-tracked fixes and releases rather than extended secrecy. That shift matters because embargoes are meant to protect users while a fix is prepared. But if AI makes discovery cheap and fast, a long embargo may only delay defense while the flaw is already exposed. text: Spot $BTC ETFs just pushed October back into the red. Thursday saw $635.6 million in net outflows, the biggest single-day exit for Bitcoin ETFs this month, and that was enough to swing October’s overall flow to a loss of about $176 million. The size of the move stands out. One session’s redemption wiped out the month’s positive flow, turning the headline number negative and putting ETF demand back under scrutiny. It was not only a Bitcoin story. Ethereum and Solana funds also saw outflows during the same period, pointing to pressure across major crypto ETF products. What drove Thursday’s exits is not confirmed. For now, the market is left watching whether this was a one-day flush or the start of a deeper pullback in ETF appetite. The crypto connection is part of the origin story. Several neoclouds began in digital-asset mining before moving toward AI compute. text: SoFi is rolling out $SOFIE, a tokenized deposit designed to mirror a $1 balance held at SoFi Bank while paying 4.40% APY. The product pairs yield with FDIC insurance, a combination ordinary stablecoins do not offer. Each token represents a $1 deposit at SoFi Bank. That one-to-one link is the core of the design: the token is meant to function as a digital claim on a bank deposit rather than a separate crypto asset backed by reserves. The standout feature is convertibility. Holders can turn the tokenized deposit into a stablecoin, creating a bridge between a bank-backed yield product and a digital-dollar format. The contrast with standard stablecoins is sharp. Most stablecoins focus on price stability; SoFi's token adds an APY and federal deposit insurance. Key details remain unconfirmed. text: Citi has cut its 12-month Bitcoin target to $82,000 from $112,000, the second reduction to its forecast in 2026. The move lands with $BTC trading around $60,041, up 2.91% on the day, as the bank reassesses the forces that previously pushed the market higher. The biggest change is Citi’s view on Bitcoin ETFs. It had expected $10 billion of net inflows over the coming year; it now projects zero. That shift follows heavy withdrawals from BTC funds, including roughly $3.3 billion in 2026 and $4 billion in June alone—the worst month on record for the products. Citi’s analysts linked the downgrade to softer investor demand, negative ETF flows and delayed U.S. crypto legislation. They also flagged a specific risk: digital asset treasury companies that have accumulated bitcoin could begin selling. text: Wavespace, a Eurozone-focused Bitcoin neobank, says its self-custodial debit card is now MiCA-compliant. The card is built for $BTC spending through the Lightning Network and is designed to avoid the usual preloaded custodial balance model that has limited crypto debit cards. Instead of parking coins on a card account, users connect a self-hosted Lightning node via Nostr Wallet Connect, or NWC, a protocol documented as NIP-47. The setup works with a minimum balance trigger. A user might set a $200 floor; when the card is used over the VISA network, Wavespace pulls sats from the user’s self-custodial wallet to top up the card. That cuts custodial exchange risk and keeps the user exposed to Bitcoin, while automating the spending process. text: Bitcoin holders often face a simple choice: sell $BTC for cash or keep holding and miss out on liquidity. Bitcoin-backed loans offer a third path—pledge BTC as collateral and borrow cash or stablecoins without giving up exposure to the asset. The structure is straightforward. A borrower locks BTC with a lender or protocol and receives a loan against it. The BTC stays tied up as collateral, while the borrower gets liquidity up front. The key variable is the loan-to-value ratio, or LTV. It sets how much can be borrowed relative to the BTC collateral. A higher LTV means more cash, but it also leaves a thinner cushion if the market moves against the borrower. That cushion matters because of liquidations. If the price of BTC falls, the LTV rises. Orchestra’s agents are focused on drug programs, not consumer chat, which makes the acquisition a direct play for biotech workflows. Rosalind gives those agents a home inside OpenAI’s broader life sciences push. text: J.P. Morgan Asset Management has put a long-term return estimate on Bitcoin for the first time, projecting 10% annual gains over 10 to 15 years in its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions. The figure gives $BTC a formal benchmark from a major traditional asset manager. The caveat is just as important: the firm is not adding Bitcoin to its main portfolio models. That separates a research projection from an allocation recommendation. For crypto watchers, the 10% number matters because it frames Bitcoin against other long-term assets in institutional planning. It also shows that large asset managers are now willing to model Bitcoin even while staying cautious. What remains unconfirmed is how J.P. text: A wallet connected to the Drift exploit has moved roughly $61 million in $ETH into Tornado Cash, a mixer designed to obscure the trail of on-chain funds. The transfer involved 25,700 ETH pushed through the mixer in just two hours. That rapid burst came from an attacker tied to April's $295 million Drift heist, which has been described as North Korea-linked. Even after routing the $61 million, the wallet still controls about $198 million, leaving a large share of the stolen funds outside the mixer for now. The scale of the remaining balance keeps attention on how the funds may be moved next, and whether more Ethereum will follow the same path through Tornado Cash. text: Switzerland has approved its first retail fund that holds $BTC directly, giving regulated retail investors a new path to Bitcoin exposure. The green light came from Swiss regulator FINMA. The approval is not a blanket relaxation. FINMA waived the fund’s diversification rules, a condition that would otherwise constrain a vehicle concentrated in a single asset. That waiver is the structural exception that lets the direct-Bitcoin format fit the retail fund framework. At the same time, FINMA pressed hard on custody and investor-protection safeguards. The regulator’s conditions focus on how the Bitcoin is held and how retail holders are protected, making those operational standards central to the approval rather than afterthoughts. text: $BTC’s next soft fork is partly about patching four legacy bugs, and Matt Corallo says the process could feel like a practice run. The work is not just maintenance. Corallo frames it as rebuilding the coordination habits around Bitcoin soft forks. That matters because a soft fork is a coordination exercise as much as a code change. A timeline and the specific bugs were not confirmed. If you hold $BTC or follow Bitcoin governance, this could be one to watch for how the community practices review and coordination — not as a signal of any price move. The takeaway: four legacy bugs, one rehearsal for Bitcoin’s next soft fork. text: Things get really clear when the market breaks a major zone. How? You basically have two options. Either you wait for price to come down to a very important zone and give you a deeper discount before buying, or you wait for the market to reclaim the levels it broke with strong volume. Altcoins drop another 10–15–20%, BTC goes through another capitulation, and then you look for buying opportunities. That's it. Two plans. Either the market shows strength, or you get a deeper discount. Nothing in between. Just relax, sit on the sidelines, and watch the market. Whichever setup plays out first, we'll react accordingly. text: Order book imbalance shows the net size of bids versus asks at each price level, revealing where resting liquidity sits. Tape noise is the stream of small, fast trades that often cancel out and carry little information. A large buy wall at $76,700 for BTC may look bullish, but if the tape shows mostly small market buys hitting it, the wall is likely absorbing pressure rather than signaling demand. Framework: weigh structural depth against flow aggression. Imbalance tells you where orders rest; tape tells you who is moving them. Use both, never one in isolation. These figures are concrete, but they are also noisy. ETF flows are better understood as a slow variable. text: Spot vs perpetual futures divergence is a behavior signal, not a price predictor. Spot reflects actual buying and selling of the asset. Perp prices embed funding rates and leverage positioning, so they can trade at a premium or discount to spot. Observation: when perp funding stays deeply positive while spot volume dries up, longs are paying to hold exposure without fresh spot demand. That is a crowded trade, not confirmation of strength. Conversely, spot accumulation with flat or negative funding suggests quiet buying while speculators are under-levered or short. Concrete frame: compare BTC spot price to the nearest BTC perpetual contract, then check funding rate and spot volume together. Divergence without volume is noise. text: Position sizing under uncertainty: risk a fixed percentage of capital per trade, not a fixed dollar amount. If BTC is at $80,372 and you risk 1% of a $10,000 account, your stop-loss distance determines position size, not the asset price. A wider stop means a smaller position; a tighter stop means a larger one. This keeps drawdowns comparable across BTC, ETH, or SOL regardless of volatility. The trade-off is that tight stops can get shaken out by normal crypto noise, while wide stops require tiny sizes that may feel meaningless. Size for the worst case, not the best case. text: Open interest is one of the most cited yet misunderstood metrics in crypto derivatives. It measures the total number of unsettled futures or perpetual contracts outstanding across an exchange. Unlike spot volume, open interest does not tell you whether traders are bullish or bearish; it only tells you how much capital is currently at risk in open positions. A durable framework for reading open interest starts with three steps. First, establish the baseline. Open interest should always be evaluated against price action and funding rates. Rising open interest alongside rising price suggests new capital is entering long positions, which can confirm trend strength. Rising open interest alongside falling price suggests new short positions are being opened, which can confirm downside pressure. Second, look for divergence. text: Most crypto education focuses on price charts. A more durable lens is operational risk: who holds the keys, who can fail, and what breaks when they do. Use three buckets. 1. Custody risk: self-custody means you bear key management; third-party custody shifts it to the platform but adds counterparty exposure. 2. Counterparty risk: the borrower, exchange, or issuer may not return your funds. 3. Operational risk: code bugs, upgrade failures, and security delays can halt or drain systems even when prices are stable. Concrete example: Ethereum recently delayed the Glamsterdam Hoodi testnet after ChainSecurity flagged 13 real-world smart contracts potentially affected by gas changes. That is operational risk visible before mainnet impact, not a price signal. Takeaway: evaluate custody, counterparty, and operational layers separately.
